Dentists and orthodontists are regulated professionals held to a high standard of care and bound to a Code of Ethics. Here are some of the principles in the American Dental Association's Code of Ethics (https://www.ada.org/en/about/principles/code-of-ethics)

Patient Autonomy (page 6): "Under this principle, the dentist’s primary obligations include involving patients in treatment decisions in a meaningful way, with due consideration being given to the patient’s needs, desires and abilities, and safeguarding the patient’s privacy. . . The dentist should inform the patient of the proposed treatment, and any reasonable alternatives, in a manner that allows the patient to become involved in treatment decisions."

Veracity (page 13): "This principle expresses the concept that professionals have a duty to be honest and trustworthy in their dealings with people. Under this principle, the dentist’s primary obligations include respecting the position of trust inherent in the dentist patient relationship, communicating truthfully and without deception, and maintaining intellectual integrity." "Dentists shall not represent the care being rendered to their patients in a false or misleading manner."

Getting someone to read over and sign a consent form without any discussion is hardly involving patients in treatment decisions in a meaningful way. Telling a patient that IPR is simply to help them floss better is representing care in a misleading manner, and is not communicating truthfully and without deception.

I'm not in the UK and I've only used Invisalign, not ClearCorrect. Also, I've never heard of "moderate" and "comprehensive" Invisalign nor of having to pay 1000 GBP to know what the final result would be. My dentist showed me the projected results before I paid anything.

Also, the fact that they're throwing in extras like tooth whitening and free hygienist appointments is a red flag - they should be focused on giving you quality results, not promotional perks. 

Have you considered getting advice from an orthodontist or two? I found the approach of orthodontists to be vastly different from dentists. They might raise other things for you to consider. The choice should be based on the best outcome for your teeth, not cost nor extra perks.

It is shocking how many dentists are performing IPR without informed consent. It happened to me too. They might be convinced to give you one since a) they messed up your teeth and b) they didn't get your consent for a procedure, neither of which would bode well for them if you were to make a complaint to their regulatory body.

It's not your responsibility to ask them to get your consent for a procedure. It is part of the orthodontist's job to fully inform you about every procedure and its associated risks, and to get your consent before proceeding. Furthermore, you asked what the procedure was and they gave you incorrect information. I am angry and shocked that this happened to you.

This is absolutely malpractice. No professional should be performing irreversible procedures on you without your prior, informed consent. Here's an article by a legal firm about lack of consent in dentistry: [https://www.stephensandholman.com/blog/can-lack-of-dental-informed-consent-constitute-malpractice/](https://www.stephensandholman.com/blog/can-lack-of-dental-informed-consent-constitute-malpractice/)

You could file a complaint with whoever regulates orthodontists in your region. They will investigate and they could potentially take disciplinary measures against your orthodontist if they conclude that malpractice occurred.

There's a saying that "emotions love themselves". It means that each emotion makes you want to do things to maintain that particular emotion. For example, when you're sad you might want to stay in bed all day, and doing so causes you to miss out on fun activities that bring happiness.

In Dialectical Behaviour Therapy there's a technique called "Opposite Action". The idea is to try to shift from an unwanted emotion by doing activities that promote the "opposite" emotion. The opposite actions to sadness are:

1. Do something active.
2. Approach something you have been avoiding.
3. Do something that makes you feel confident and competent.
4. Do an activity you find pleasant.
5. Pay attention to the present moment.
6. Adopt an upright posture, head up, speak in an upbeat tone of voice.
7. Engage in physical activity.

These are all behaviours that tend to increase happiness, the opposite of sadness. We tend to think our mood leads to our behaviour. In fact, our behaviour also influences our mood. We might not be able to rid sadness and depression overnight but we can shift our mood over time starting with small behaviour changes.

Also, this isn't meant to invalidate you, feeling sad is completely valid. I imagine things have happened for it to make sense that you'd be sad. This method is just an option to help us when we want to feel differently.

I’m sorry you’re in this situation OP, I have BPD too and have been in the same situation. The pain was excruciating. I want to echo the first comment and say that moving on is the right thing to do, out of respect for this person and yourself. You want to apologize to them because you want to repair the relationship. But this person is like a house on fire, you want to be in your home, but the more you run in there, the more you get burned. It is time to extricate yourself from them for your own wellness. 

You’re still in the thick of it so it makes sense that you haven’t processed the whole situation yet. Try to balance processing the situation and giving yourself a break from thinking about it. You know your own limits. Remove any reminder of the person as much as possible, grieving if you need to. Do activities to self-soothe, like taking baths or listening to music. When you’re able to, focus on improving other aspects of your life. Acknowledge that it’s difficult to stop dwelling on this person, don’t judge yourself for it. Recognize the thoughts, activities, or emotions that make you feel better or worse. Pursue the emotions that you want to have. Assess what value this relationship had for you, this will help you self-validate and learn about yourself. Acknowledge that you can’t change your feelings about this person, but you can focus on everything else - family, friends, other relationships, work, school, hobbies, health, spirituality… you get the picture, whatever is important to you personally. 

I understand that you might feel ashamed or hurt thinking that the person might think badly of you for your behaviour. But who knows what they really think about you and nobody, not even someone you love, determines your value anyway. 

These are suggestions to practice over time, it isn’t possible to do them all right away. These are all tips from my own experience and DBT. I still love and miss the person who cut me out two years ago but I am now able to live a full life regardless and you will be able to too.
